# dsh-continue-kicker

**Automatically send "continue" when a turn halts, and stop when that is not helping.**

A host-plane plugin for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). A session that hits its output-token limit just stops, silently, until somebody notices. This plugin notices: it sends one follow-up user message that tells the model to stop re-deriving its reasoning and act, and it gives up after a configurable number of kicks with no progress in between, so a task genuinely too big for its budget surfaces in the log instead of burning GPU-hours.

## What it kicks on

| Halt | Detected as | Kick |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Output budget exhausted | last `turn/end` reason `max-tokens` | "Do NOT re-derive your thinking: state your conclusion, then act. Be succinct." |
| Reasoning-only empty stop | `completed` turn whose final assistant message has no text and no tool call, with at least `emptyCompletionMinReasoningChars` of reasoning | Same "be decisive" framing |
| Failed turn (opt-in: `kickOnError`) | last `turn/end` reason `error` (the model backend dropped, a provider error) | "The previous turn failed with an error and was cut off before it finished. Please continue from where you left off." |
| Crash-orphaned turn | last `turn/end` reason `interrupted` (synthesized when a session is loaded) | "Please continue from where you left off." |

It never kicks over `aborted` (an explicit Stop, a parent or hook cancel, a disposal), `error` unless `kickOnError` is on, `blocked`, `forked`, a completed turn with real content, or a tail already followed by a user or assistant message.

Two doors feed one decision: `agent/created` (reopening a session, crash recovery) and a live watcher that re-analyses the tail `liveKickDelayMs` after every turn end, so an unattended halt is caught without anyone reopening the session. A third door is explicit: another plugin can ask for one kick of one session through the [`continueKicker` service](#provided-service-continuekicker), which runs the same decision and applies the same guards.

## Install

Installed from a git tag of this repository — it is not published to npm. Replace `<version>` with a released version (tags are named `dsh-continue-kicker-v<version>`; see [the tag list](https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tags)):

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-continue-kicker-v<version>&path:/packages/continue-kicker"
```

That installs the package into the profile and enables its bundle. If you manage the profile's `package.json` yourself, the pnpm equivalent is below — then also add `dsh-continue-kicker` to the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, because `pnpm add` alone installs the plugin without enabling it:

```sh
pnpm add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-continue-kicker-v<version>&path:/packages/continue-kicker"
```

> **Warning:** never `pnpm add dsh-continue-kicker` (or `dsh plugin add dsh-continue-kicker`) by bare name. That resolves from the npm registry, where an unscoped `dsh-*` name may belong to an unrelated author and is **not** this plugin.

Restart dsh. With no configuration it works with the defaults below.

## Configuration

Set these on the plugin's row in your own profile patch (`config:` block). **A top-level row with a `config:` block replaces the whole config object**, so list every key you want to differ from the default in the same row; unlisted keys fall back to the defaults below. The bundle's own layer carries no config for the same reason.

| Key | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cooldownMs` | `60000` | Minimum time between kicks for the same session. |
| `liveKickDelayMs` | `3000` | Delay between a live turn end and the tail re-analysis. Lets a fast manual recovery land first. |
| `maxConsecutiveKicks` | `5` | Runaway guard: after this many kicks (all flavors together, counted from the session's event log) with no normally completed turn and no genuine user message in between, the plugin stops kicking that session and logs an error. `0` disables kicking entirely, quietly (the `kickOn*` flags are the finer-grained off switches). |
| `kickOnInterrupted` | `true` | Kick crash-orphaned turns. |
| `kickOnMaxTokens` | `true` | Kick output-token-limit halts. |
| `kickOnEmptyCompletion` | `true` | Kick reasoning-only completed turns. |
| `kickOnError` | `false` | Kick turns that ended with `reason.kind: 'error'`. Off by default because blindly retrying a failing backend can loop; the runaway guard and cooldown bound it. You would want it for unattended work on a backend that drops now and then (a gateway restart, a network blip): the session resumes by itself once the backend is back instead of sitting dead until someone notices. |
| `includeSubagents` | `false` | Also kick delegated child sessions (`origin: subagent` or `delegationDepth > 0`). Off by default: auto-kicking a child fights the parent's own delegation and retry flow. |
| `logToStderr` | `false` | Write this plugin's log lines to stderr (see Logging). Needed to see them at all on dsh 0.2.0-rc.2. |
| `emptyCompletionMinReasoningChars` | `500` | Reasoning length below which a content-empty completed turn is left alone. |
| `interruptedKickText` | built in | Text sent for an interrupted turn. |
| `maxTokensKickText` | built in | Text sent for a max-tokens halt. Forbids re-deriving the lost reasoning; a plain "please continue" invites another long think straight back into the wall. |
| `emptyCompletionKickText` | built in | Text sent for a reasoning-only empty stop. |
| `errorKickText` | built in | Text sent for a failed turn when `kickOnError` is on. |

Resolution lives in [`src/config.mjs`](./src/config.mjs) and is [tested](./test/config.test.mjs). An unknown key, a string where a number belongs, or an empty text prints one warning at boot and falls back to the default.

Example row (the default for `maxConsecutiveKicks` is 5; 3 here is just an example):

```yaml
- id: continue-kicker
  name: dsh-continue-kicker
  config:
    cooldownMs: 60000
    liveKickDelayMs: 3000
    maxConsecutiveKicks: 3
    kickOnInterrupted: true
    kickOnMaxTokens: true
    kickOnEmptyCompletion: true
    kickOnError: true
    includeSubagents: false
    logToStderr: true
```

## Which turn-end reasons kick

From `TurnEndReasonMap` in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session`:

| `reason.kind` | Meaning | Kicked? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max-tokens` | output budget hit | yes, `kickOnMaxTokens` |
| `interrupted` | crash-orphaned turn closed on load | yes, `kickOnInterrupted` |
| `completed` | model stopped itself | only a reasoning-only empty one, `kickOnEmptyCompletion` |
| `error` | the turn failed (`error` holds message and code) | yes, only with `kickOnError` |
| `aborted` | cancelled on purpose (`user`, `parent`, `hook`, `disposed`, `legacy`) | never |
| `blocked` | a step was rejected before running | never |
| `forked` | fork-seed marker, never emitted live | never |

## The runaway guard

A kick can itself end in the same halt, so the plugin counts kicks and stops at `maxConsecutiveKicks`.

The count is derived from the session's own event log on every analysis, not kept in memory, so it survives a dsh restart and the live and reopen paths always agree. It is the number of this plugin's kick messages (source kind `plugin:continue-kicker`; the retired bare `plugin` kind counts only when it names this plugin and carries one of the known kick texts) found walking back from the end of the log, up to the nearest reset signal:

- a **genuine user message**: source kind `user` and nothing else. The plugin's own kicks and any other producer's user-role messages (goals, other plugins) neither reset nor count.
- a turn that **completed normally**. A reasoning-only completion is a kickable halt, not progress, so it does not reset.

Every flavor counts together: max-tokens, empty-completion, error and interrupted. So the cap also bounds a crash loop: a session that keeps getting killed mid-turn and resumed stops being resumed after `maxConsecutiveKicks` kicks until a user message or a completed turn arrives. At the cap the plugin logs an error naming the session ("needs human attention") and does not kick. Only the cooldown timestamp is in memory; a restart forgets it, which at worst allows one extra kick that the stateless cap still bounds.

Changed from 0.1.0: the old reset fired only when a genuine user message was the *last* event, but a halted turn always ends in `turn/end`, so a new prompt after the cap never reset it; the count lived in memory and was lost on restart; and interrupted kicks were not counted at all.

The kick is written with source kind `plugin:continue-kicker`. Session format V4 refuses the bare kind `plugin`, so a session carrying such a message could not be reopened after a restart.

## Provided service: `continueKicker`

Besides watching sessions on its own, the plugin provides a service named `continueKicker` so another plugin that owns a session's lifecycle can ask for one explicit recovery kick instead of waiting for the automatic doors. `dsh-kanban` uses it: when a role turn halts, the engine asks for a kick and waits for the result, so the recovery is part of the workflow rather than something that happens to a parked session.

```js
const kicker = ctx.get('continueKicker')   // undefined when this plugin is not installed
```

| Member | Shape | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | `1` | the contract version. It goes up only on a breaking change; a consumer that sees an unknown version should treat the details as unreliable. |
| `kick(sessionId, options?)` | `(string, { bypassCooldown?: boolean }) => result` | runs one decision for one live session and sends the kick if it is due. Synchronous; never throws. |

`kick` returns one of:

| Result | When |
| --- | --- |
| `{ kicked: true, flavor, consecutive }` | a kick was sent. `flavor` is `max-tokens`, `interrupted`, `empty-completion` or `error`; `consecutive` is this kick's number in the runaway count. |
| `{ kicked: false, why }` | nothing was sent: the session is not live, its tail is not a kickable halt, the halt's `kickOn*` switch is off, the session is an excluded subagent, or the cooldown is running. |
| `{ kicked: false, why, stopped: true }` | the runaway guard declined: this session has already had `maxConsecutiveKicks` kicks with no progress and needs a human. |

The service is the **same decision, not a second one**: `kick()` runs `decide()` over the session's own event log with this plugin's resolved settings, sends the same message with the same `plugin:continue-kicker` source kind, records the same cooldown, and is bounded by the same runaway counter. A caller therefore gets the plugin's policy instead of a private copy of it, and the automatic doors keep working alongside it — a kick sent through the service lands in the log like any other, so the watcher's delayed re-analysis of the same halt sees a kick already awaiting its result and does nothing.

`bypassCooldown: true` opens only the cooldown gate. It exists because a caller that just watched a turn fail is asking for recovery, not re-analysing a halt it kicked a second ago; every other gate (the per-kind switches, the subagent scope, `maxConsecutiveKicks`) still applies.

One consequence of removing that spacing is worth knowing about: a kick message only lands in the session's event log when the turn it starts claims it, so a caller that asks for kicks back to back can be reading a log one kick behind its own sending. The guard takes the higher of the log count and the kicks this process has actually sent, so the lag cannot buy an extra kick; a genuine user message or a normally completed turn resets both together.

**The service is optional for the consumer.** A caller must resolve it lazily (`ctx.get` at use time, not at boot), duck-type `typeof kicker?.kick === 'function'`, and degrade to its own behaviour when it is absent — the same rule `dsh-kanban` follows for the `betterGitWorktree` service. Nothing here requires a caller: with no consumer installed the plugin behaves exactly as before.

## Logging

Every decision, kick or skip, is logged with its reason, through the host logger under the name `continue-kicker`.

**Where those lines go (dsh 0.2.0-rc.2):** nowhere you can read. The harness registers no console or file exporter on the logger; plugin lines only land in an in-memory ring buffer (`ctx.logger.buffer`, 1000 entries) that nothing displays, and only startup warnings and errors are surfaced, inside a startup failure. So `journalctl -u dsh | grep continue-kicker` finds nothing by default. Set `logToStderr: true` and the plugin registers its own exporter that writes only its own lines to stderr, which a service manager (journald under systemd) captures:

```
2026-10-15T18:28:05.590Z INFO continue-kicker created: kicked session s1 (flavor=max-tokens, consecutive=1)
```

The kick itself is also visible in the conversation as a notice row ("Auto-resumed after a max-tokens halt (2/5)"), but the "needs human attention" error at the cap appears only in the log. A general fix (surface plugin logs in the harness) belongs upstream or in a separate plugin.

## Compatibility

Requires dsh 0.2.0-rc.2 or later. Declared in `package.json` under `engines.dsh` and on every `@deepseek-ai/dsh*` peer as `>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0-0 || >=0.3.0-0`. dsh checks these ranges itself, counting prereleases, so it accepts every harness build from 0.2.0-rc.2 on; on a harness outside them `dsh plugin add` refuses the install, and a profile that already has it skips the bundle with a log line. pnpm's own peer check is narrower: it admits only `0.2.0-rc.*` and `0.3.0-*` prereleases (plus every stable release from 0.2.0), so on other prereleases it reports a peer mismatch that dsh does not.

## Development

```sh
node --test packages/continue-kicker/test/*.test.mjs   # decisions + config
node scripts/verify.mjs --package dsh-continue-kicker  # release contract
node scripts/compose-smoke.mjs continue-kicker         # real dsh composition
```

`src/decide.mjs` and `src/config.mjs` import nothing from dsh; `src/host.mjs` is the thin Cordis wiring. See [`../../docs/authoring.md`](../../docs/authoring.md).

# dsh-plugins

Public [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) plugins by [Chris Johnson](https://github.com/chrisjohnson). One repository, independently installable plugins — each with its own README, its own tests, its own changelog and its own version.

## Install

**Nothing here is published to npm.** Every release is a git tag on this repository, named `<package>-v<version>` (for example `dsh-model-switch-v0.2.1`), and you install a plugin by pinning that tag plus the package's subdirectory:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#<package>-v<version>&path:/packages/<dir>"
```

`dsh plugin add` hands that spec to pnpm and also lists the package under the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, which is what activates its configuration layer. If you manage a profile's `package.json` yourself, the same spec works with pnpm directly — but then add the package name to `dsh.profile.bundles` by hand, because a plain `pnpm add` installs the plugin without enabling it:

```sh
pnpm add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#<package>-v<version>&path:/packages/<dir>"
```

Pick the tag from [the repository's tags](https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tags); `<dir>` is the folder under `packages/` in the index below.

> **Warning — do not install these by bare name.** `pnpm add dsh-model-switch` (or `dsh plugin add dsh-model-switch`) resolves against the npm registry, and the npm package called `dsh-model-switch` belongs to an unrelated author: it is **not** this plugin. The same can happen to any unscoped `dsh-*` name. Always use the git-tag spec above.

## Index

| Plugin | What it is for | Latest | Directory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **[dsh-model-switch](./packages/model-switch/)** | Let the agent switch its own model mid-session, with a context-window fit guard so neither it nor a human in the composer can strand a conversation on a model too small to read it. | 0.2.1 | `packages/model-switch` |
| **[dsh-image-search-searxng](./packages/image-search-searxng/)** | A model-facing `image_search` tool over your own SearXNG, rendered inline in the Web GUI. | 0.2.0 | `packages/image-search-searxng` |
| **[dsh-continue-kicker](./packages/continue-kicker/)** | Automatically send "continue" when a turn halts on the output-token limit (or after a crash, or on a reasoning-only empty stop), with a runaway guard that stops after repeated kicks with no progress. | 0.2.0 | `packages/continue-kicker` |
| **[dsh-loop-watchdog](./packages/loop-watchdog/)** | Detect an agent stuck in a loop before each step (a deterministic repetition check plus an optional model judge), keep an audit ledger of every check, optionally steer the session, and chart the ledger in a `dsh-better-sidebar` panel. | 0.1.0 | `packages/loop-watchdog` |
| **[dsh-scheduled-queue](./packages/scheduled-queue/)** | Schedule the composer's draft to be sent to its own session later, with a per-session dock to edit, cancel or send now. Runs alongside the official schedule bundle. | 0.1.0 | `packages/scheduled-queue` |
| **[dsh-kanban](./packages/kanban/)** | Ticket-centric work organizer and code-driven workflow engine: a local SQLite board whose phases spawn sandboxed role sessions, gate on per-provider capacity, verify machine-readable conditions, and record a complete time/token ledger. | 0.1.0 | `packages/kanban` |
| **[dsh-model-capacity](./packages/model-capacity/)** | Process-wide, per-provider model-call capacity: every call — an interactive turn or a subagent child's — queues FIFO for its provider, and a panel inspects active leases and waiters. | 0.4.0 | `packages/model-capacity` |
| **[dsh-better-git-worktree](./packages/better-git-worktree/)** | Run a session in its own self-contained git working copy: a composer Worktree switch, a `worktree_convert` tool, session-list status badges, a header menu, and an archive prompt that decides the working copy's fate. | 0.1.1 | `packages/better-git-worktree` |
| **[dsh-session-cost](./packages/session-cost/)** | A compact estimated-cost badge in the composer stats bar: reads the session billed-token buckets and prices them with public models.dev rates, hidden at $0. | 0.1.0 | `packages/session-cost` |
| **[dsh-math-literal](./packages/math-literal/)** | Keeps single-`$` dollars literal in web chat: unpaired `$` in settled markdown renders as a literal dollar sign (matching the streaming arm) instead of opening an inline-math pair, while real math and code regions are untouched. | 0.1.0 | `packages/math-literal` |
| **[dsh-browser](./packages/browser/)** | One browser context per DSH session on a single shared remote Browserless connection for `dsh-playwright-browser`'s tools, with reconnect after a dropped connection, context cleanup when a session ends, and an announced local fallback. | 0.1.0 | `packages/browser` |

Install lines for the latest release of each package:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-model-switch-v0.2.1&path:/packages/model-switch"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-image-search-searxng-v0.2.0&path:/packages/image-search-searxng"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-continue-kicker-v0.2.0&path:/packages/continue-kicker"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-loop-watchdog-v0.1.0&path:/packages/loop-watchdog"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-scheduled-queue-v0.1.0&path:/packages/scheduled-queue"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-kanban-v0.1.0&path:/packages/kanban"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-model-capacity-v0.4.0&path:/packages/model-capacity"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-better-git-worktree-v0.1.1&path:/packages/better-git-worktree"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-session-cost-v0.1.0&path:/packages/session-cost"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-math-literal-v0.1.0&path:/packages/math-literal"
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-browser-v0.1.0&path:/packages/browser"
```

Each package's README is the contract: what it does, every configuration key and what happens when it is unset, how it fails, how to install it, and how to run its checks. Nothing important lives only here.

## Releases

1. A release is a normal pull request that bumps one package's version and moves its CHANGELOG `Unreleased` entry under that version.
2. After it merges, the tag `<package>-v<version>` is cut on that merge commit and pushed. Nothing is committed directly to `main`.
3. Consumers pin the tag with the install spec above. A tag is never moved or rewritten once pushed.

Details: [docs/releasing.md](./docs/releasing.md).

## What "a plugin from this repo" means

- **Plain ESM, no build step.** `git clone && npm test` works with nothing installed. No bundler, no TypeScript layer, no generated client — what the harness loads is what is in `src/`.
- **Every plugin declares `dsh.bundle.patch`**, so one command installs *and* activates it; nothing here needs a hand-edited `cordis.yml`.
- **Deployment-specific values are configuration, never defaults.** A plugin that "works on my machine" because it hard-codes my provider ids is broken for everyone else. `node scripts/verify.mjs` fails the build on author-local paths and provider ids.
- **Nothing is required to be configured.** Optional features report themselves unavailable and name the key that enables them, instead of throwing at boot or failing at first use.
- **Every decision worth testing lives in a module that imports nothing from dsh**, which is what makes the tests real rather than decorative.

## Checking this repository

```sh
npm run check          # verify + hook gate + all tests, no install needed
node scripts/verify.mjs            # the release contract (see below)
node scripts/compose-smoke.mjs     # install into a throwaway profile, import, compose
```

`scripts/verify.mjs` is the interesting one: it enforces the rules that make a plugin installable and trustworthy — `dsh.bundle.patch` present and loading the package by name, `dsh.client` matched by an `./client` export, one harness peer range across every package (`>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0-0 || >=0.3.0-0`; dsh checks it with prereleases included, while plain node-semver/pnpm admit only `0.2.0-rc.*` and `0.3.0-*` prereleases from it), every shipped file inside the `files` allowlist (all a git-tag install ships), a git-tag install line (and no bare-name one) in every package README, every config key documented in its README, every package listed in the index above, and no deployment leakage. It runs on CI for every push and it runs on a bare clone.

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md). If you are an agent working in this repository, read [AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md) first; it is short and it exists because these plugins run with your user's credentials.

For how these plugins get developed, tested against a live harness, released and consumed by the deployment they came from, see [docs/testing.md](./docs/testing.md) and [docs/releasing.md](./docs/releasing.md).

## License

MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

evidence.readmeExcerpt: # dsh-image-search-searxng **Give the agent image search against a SearXNG you already run — and give the user the pictures inline.** A single model-facing `image_search` tool for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness), pointed at the `images` category of your own [SearXNG](https://docs.searxng.org/) instance. No API key vendor, no third party in the request path, nothing leaves your network that you did not already let SearXNG reach. ``` You: find a wiring diagram for a NEMA 14-50 receptacle Agent: [image_search] → 3 results, each a markdown image link GUI: renders them as real inline pictures ``` ## Install Installed from a git tag of this repository — it is not published to npm. Replace `` with a released version (tags are named `dsh-image-search-searxng-v`; see [the tag list](https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tags)): ```sh dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-image-search-searxng-v&path:/packages/image-search-searxng" ``` That installs the package into the profile and enables its bundle. If you manage the profile's `package.json` yourself, the pnpm equivalent is below — then also add `dsh-image-search-searxng` to the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, because `pnpm add` alone installs the plugin without enabling it: ```sh pnpm add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-image-search-searxng-v&path:/packages/image-search-searxng" ``` > **Warning:** never install this plugin by bare name from the npm registry. Nothing from this repository is published there, so whatever a bare `pnpm add dsh-image-search-searxng` resolves to — now or later — is not this plugin. (The sibling name `dsh-model-switch` is already taken on npm by an unrelated author.) Restart dsh. The tool is then available to every agent preset — the bundle's patch layer mounts the plugin at the profile level, so no per-preset `agent.cordis.yml` editing is involved. Zero configuration is required if your SearXNG answers on `http://localhost:8888`. ## Configuration | Key | Environment | Default | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `baseURL` | `SEARXNG_BASE_URL` | `http://localhost:8888` | Where your SearXNG lives. Trailing slashes are trimmed; a value that is not an `http(s)` URL is rejected at boot rather than failing at the first search. | | `apiKey` | `SEARXNG_API_KEY` | — | Sent as `preference[api_key]`, for SearXNG instances with API support enabled. | | `maxResults` | `SEARXNG_NUM_RESULTS` | `8` | Default result count the model gets if it does not ask. A per-call `maxResults` argument still wins, clamped to 1–30. | Precedence is **config → environment → default**. To override in your profile patch, add the keys to the row this plugin inserts: ```yaml - id: image-search-searxng name: dsh-image-search-searxng config: baseURL: http://searxng.internal:8080 maxResults: 5 ``` If the plugin is already mounted by its bundle, a config-only row keyed by `id` is enough, and `!!js` lets the row pass environment variables through. Unset variables arrive as `undefined` and fall back exactly as an absent key would: ```yaml - id: image-search-searxng config: baseURL: !!js process.env.SEARXNG_BASE_URL ``` One caveat worth knowing about patch layers generally: a patch **replaces a row's entire `config` object**, it does not deep-merge. Restating `baseURL` in a later layer drops `apiKey` unless you restate that too — which is why this plugin ships its row with no `config` block at all and resolves defaults in code. ## What the model actually receives Titles, source pages, resolutions, and one markdown image link per result: ``` 1. **NEMA 14-50 wiring** ![NEMA 14-50 wiring](https://example.com/diagram.png) Source: https://example.com/receptacles Resolution: 1024x768 ``` The tool's canonical value is `{ results: [{ title?, imgSrc, sourceUrl, resolution? }] }`, and its model-facing result is that list rendered as a single `text` content block — no `image` blocks, no attachments. The plugin writes no session messages of its own. That link is not decoration. dsh's own `dsh-client-ui-primitives` renderer turns `![alt](url)` into a real `` for any `http(s)` URL — there is no domain allowlist — and falls back to alt text only when the browser's own image request fails (hotlink protection, dead link). So results appear as pictures whenever the source host cooperates, with no code-level distinction between the two cases. The tool description tells the model to copy the links verbatim precisely because rewriting one into a plain `[text](url)` link removes the picture. ## Why a separate tool instead of extending `web_search` Because the shared web seam has nowhere to put an image. `WebSearchRequest` and `WebSearchSource` in `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web` carry no category and no image fields, so adding them means patching multiple upstream packages that every future dsh upgrade would then have to be re-verified against. A standalone tool with its own schema costs one registration and stays working across upgrades. This is the same shape `dsh-web-search-searxng` chose. ## What this plugin deliberately does not do - **It does not show the model the images.** The model receives text: titles and URLs. It cannot describe, compare, or verify what is depicted, and the tool description says so in as many words, because "I looked at the diagram and it shows…" is otherwise a very tempting hallucination. - **It does not fetch images through your model's attachment pipeline.** Real image *attachments* would route arbitrary third-party URLs through the vision/attachment path — a much larger blast radius than "the user can see search results" warrants. - **It does not fall back to a hosted search API.** If SearXNG is unreachable the tool call fails with the HTTP status, rather than silently querying somebody else's service. ## Compatibility Requires dsh 0.2.0-rc.2 or later. Declared in `package.json` under `engines.dsh` and on the `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` peer as `>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0-0 || >=0.3.0-0`. dsh checks the range itself, counting prereleases, so it accepts every harness build from 0.2.0-rc.2 on; on a harness outside it `dsh plugin add` refuses the install, and a profile that already has it skips the bundle with a log line. pnpm's own peer check is narrower: it admits only `0.2.0-rc.*` and `0.3.0-*` prereleases (plus every stable release from 0.2.0), so on other prereleases it reports a peer mismatch that dsh does not. ## Development The plugin is plain ESM with no build step. ```sh node --test packages/image-search-searxng/test/*.test.mjs # logic, no dsh needed node scripts/verify.mjs --package dsh-image-search-searxng # release contract node scripts/compose-smoke.mjs image-search-searxng # real dsh composition ``` `src/searxng.mjs` holds the logic and the tests; `src/index.mjs` is the Cordis wiring. The split is not ceremony — it is what lets the tests run before anything is installed. See [`../../docs/authoring.md`](../../docs/authoring.md). ## License MIT # dsh-plugins Public [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) plugins by [Chris Johnson](https://github.com/chrisjohnson). One repository, independently installable plugins — each with its own README, its own tests, its own changelog and its own version. ## Install **Nothing here is published to npm.** Every release is a git tag on this repository, named `-v` (for example `dsh-model-switch-v0.2.1`), and you install a plugin by pinning that tag plus the package's subdirectory: ```sh dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#-v&path:/packages/" ``` `dsh plugin add` hands that spec to pnpm and also lists the package under the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, which is what activates its configuration layer. it is unset, how it fails, how to install it, and how to run its checks. Nothing important lives only here. ## Releases 1. A release is a normal pull request that bumps one package's version and moves its CHANGELOG `Unreleased` entry under that version. 2. After it merges, the tag `-v` is cut on that merge commit and pushed. Nothing is committed directly to `main`. 3. Consumers pin the tag with the install spec above. A tag is never moved or rewritten once pushed. Details: [docs/releasing.md](./docs/releasing.md). ## What "a plugin from this repo" means - **Plain ESM, no build step.** `git clone && npm test` works with nothing installed. No bundler, no TypeScript layer, no generated client — what the harness loads is what is in `src/`. - **Every plugin declares `dsh.bundle.patch`**, so one command installs *and* activates it; nothing here needs a hand-edited `cordis.yml`. - **Deployment-specific values are configuration, never defaults.** A plugin that "works on my machine" because it hard-codes my provider ids is broken for everyone else. `node scripts/verify.mjs` fails the build on author-local paths and provider ids. - **Nothing is required to be configured.** Optional features report themselves unavailable and name the key that enables them, instead of throwing at boot or failing at first use. - **Every decision worth testing lives in a module that imports nothing from dsh**, which is what makes the tests real rather than decorative. ## Checking this repository ```sh npm run check # verify + hook gate + all tests, no install needed node scripts/verify.mjs # the release contract (see below) node scripts/compose-smoke.mjs # install into a throwaway profile, import, compose ``` `scripts/verify.mjs` is the interesting one: it enforces the rules that make a plugin installable and trustworthy — `dsh.bundle.patch` present and loading the package by name, `dsh.client` matched by an `./client` export, one harness peer range across every package (`>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0-0 || >=0.3.0-0`; dsh checks it with prereleases included, while plain node-semver/pnpm admit only `0.2.0-rc.*` and `0.3.0-*` prereleases from it), every shipped file inside the `files` allowlist (all a git-tag install ships), a git-tag install line (and no bare-name one) in every package README, every config key documented in its README, every package listed in the index above, and no deployment leakage. evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# dsh-kanban

A ticket-centric workflow plugin for DeepSeek Harness. Tickets live in SQLite;
code drives them through one flat plan session and one build session that
implements, reviews and then carries approval, with a code-gated review result
and a human who closes the ticket. Agents return structured data by calling
tools, not by printing JSON.

## Install

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-kanban-v<version>&path:/packages/kanban"
```

The bundle mounts `id: kanban` with no config. Put the complete config section
in the deployment profile.

## Ticket flow

```text
plan session
  native ask_user_question (interactive) or self-judgement
  kanban_submit_plan
      ↓
build session
  kanban_submit_implementation
  kanban_submit_review
  fail → implement again in the same session
      ↓ review pass with one done_when row per plan id
      ↓ and acceptance_coverage for every acceptance statement
  approval — the same session, flipped to the approver phase (attention card)
  the agent hands the work over and asks; kanban_approve, kanban_discard,
  kanban_submit_plan
      ↓ approve
   done

kanban_plan (read-only) is available in every session and returns the plan,
its conditions and the latest review, so a session can re-read the contract it
is working against instead of trusting its own summary of it.
```

Approval is a **phase**, not a session. The session that wrote the code and
reviewed it is the one that asks the human what to do with it: it keeps its
workspace, its history and its tools, its phase role flips to `approver`, and it
moves onto the configured approver route. There is no separate approval session
to launch, and no second conversation to catch up on what was built.

There is no verification session. The review is checked in code against the
original plan and acceptance: every planned done_when id must be present with
met/confidence/evidence, and every acceptance statement must be covered. A
missing or incomplete review goes back to implementation. Only when that code
gate passes does the ticket enter human approval.

Columns are **intended state** — where you want the ticket to live — and the
engine never moves a ticket between them on its own. Whether work is happening
is a card-level visual status computed from live facts: a blue pulsing dot and
glow while a workflow turn is in flight, a red glowing card when the engine has
parked the ticket for a human (a failure, a question, or approval), and a plain
grey card otherwise.

Since 0.13.1 a red card also covers the wait *inside* a turn: when a session
pauses mid-turn on an unanswered approval prompt (the harness `approval/asked`
… `approval/decided` pair) or an unanswered `ask_user_question`, the card shows
**Awaiting approval** or **Waiting on you** instead of pretending work is
happening. This needs no configuration: there is no new config key, no schema
change and no tool change — the durable session log already carried the fact,
and the board now reads it.

Needs attention is a state, not a parking brake or a column. The moment any
session attached to a parked ticket starts a turn — you answering the engine's
question, driving the build by hand, or talking an approval through — the park
lifts in place and the card turns blue, and the engine will not inject a role
prompt into a session that already has a turn running. When that turn ends
without a structured submission the card returns to red with the reason it had
before; a `kanban_submit_*` call from the same turn advances the ticket as
usual.

Plan and verify sessions start once in the **standard preset**; a build session
starts in the preset the ticket chose, or the harness default when it did not
choose one. Either way a session uses its preset's natural system prompt and has
every tool that preset gives a normal session. The plugin does not rebind
presets mid-session, install a custom system prompt, or register a tool guard.
The sandbox mode follows the session's **purpose** plus the ticket's write-mode
choice: plan and verify are always read-only, and a build session runs
`read-only`, `workspace-write` (the default) or `danger-full-access` as the
ticket asked — through all three of its phases, implement, review and approval;
a phase change inside one session never moves it. If a stored preset is no
longer registered when the session spawns, the session starts in the harness
default and the ticket records a `preset_fallback` event. Workflow sessions
attach to the ticket's selected workspace and are titled `KAN-n · purpose`.

Ticket choices:

- **Planning:** `now` or `at_pickup`
- **Questions:** `interactive` (native `ask_user_question`) or `autonomous`
  (self-judgement prompt)
- **Preset:** the starting preset of the ticket's build session — the harness
  default (stored as null, so it keeps tracking future default changes) or any
  registered preset; plan and verify stay on standard
- **Write mode:** the build session's file policy — `read-only`,
  `workspace-write` (default) or `danger-full-access`; plan and verify stay
  read-only

The plan session is one flat session: it asks questions, researches, and calls
`kanban_submit_plan` when confident. A valid plan ends that session. Implement,
review and approval share one session; a complete review flips that same session
to the approver phase and asks the human what to do with the work.

### Sandbox grants (0.16.0)

A build session runs under the ticket's write mode with the ticket's workspace as
its sandbox root. Anything outside that — a lab directory, a scratch checkout, a
command the sandbox would deny — normally stops the build mid-turn to ask a human.
A plan may declare those needs up front, in an optional `sandbox` section:

```json
"sandbox": {
  "grants": {
    "paths": ["/home/dsh/dsh-lab/kan30-grant"],
    "commands": ["git push", "gh pr create"]
  },
  "checks": [
    { "path": "/home/dsh/dsh-lab/kan30-grant", "check": "test -w /home/dsh/dsh-lab/kan30-grant", "observed": "writable" }
  ]
}
```

- **A plan that declares grants parks.** The ticket stays in Plan with a
  *Plan ready: N sandbox grant(s) declared* reason and an **Approve plan**
  button on the board. Approving is the one-time grant: it lifts the park,
  records a `plan_approved` event, and the build starts with exactly these
  escalations pre-approved. A plan without grants behaves exactly as before —
  no park, no new step.
- **Matching is mechanical.** A `write`/`edit` call is covered when its
  `file_path` is a granted path or lives under it at a path-segment boundary
  (`/a/b` grants `/a/b/c`, never `/a/bc`). A `bash` call is covered when its
  command starts with a granted prefix at word boundaries (`git push` grants
  `git push origin main`, never `git pushfoo`). The matcher reads the exact
  arguments from the session's own `tool/call` event, never from the model's
  justification text.
- **The denylist is never claimable.** The check is **word-based, not
  position-based**: the command is split on whitespace and on the shell syntax
  that can hide a command from a first-token read (`(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `$`,
  backtick, `;`, `|`, `&` and newlines), quotes and backslashes are stripped, and
  if ANY resulting word — reduced to its basename and seen through wrappers like
  `sudo`, `env`, `nohup`, `timeout` and `sh -c`/`bash -c` script bodies — is
  `systemctl`, `service`, `launchctl`, `sudo`, `kill`, `pkill`, `rm` or `dd`, the
  whole call is denied; so is any line containing `rm -rf /` or `rm -fr /`. None
  of it can ever be auto-approved, not even by a grant a human approved, and a
  plan declaring one is rejected at submission with a *can never be granted*
  error. Because no position in the command is safe, a granted prefix cannot
  carry a denylisted command written in any natural shell form: a `git push`
  grant covers `git push origin main` and nothing like `git push && systemctl
  restart dsh`, `git push && (systemctl restart dsh)`, `git push && $(systemctl
  restart dsh)`, `git push && FOO=1 systemctl restart dsh` or `git push &&
  \systemctl restart dsh`. Being word-based costs false positives on purpose —
  `grep -r rm -n .` and `git commit -m "rm old path"` ask the human too — because
  a prompt is cheap and a wrong auto-approval is not.
- **The denylist is a text rule, not a sandbox.** It narrows what a grant may
  *say*; it cannot control what a granted command *does*, and three routes stay
  open by construction: an **interpreter** (a plan granting a bare `node`,
  `python3`, `perl` or `bash script.sh` prefix hands the build whatever that
  interpreter runs), an **encoded payload** (`echo <base64> | base64 -d | sh`
  hides its words from any matcher), and **indirection** (a granted command that
  reads a script or config the build wrote inside the workspace). None of these
  is reachable by string matching, so they are the human's call at plan-review
  time: read an interpreter grant as a full-access grant, look at the script a
  grant will run, and prefer the narrowest prefix that actually works.
- **Everything else still asks.** The grant approver is an agent-scoped
  `approval/request` waterfall listener registered only on build sessions
  (plan and verify sessions stay read-only and receive none). It claims only
  asks whose reason starts with `escalate sandbox to `, and it fails open:
  a malformed call, a missing plan, a terminal ticket or any exception falls
  through to the human. Grants live in the plan artifact, so a new plan
  version supersedes them, and while a ticket is parked on *Plan ready* the
  grants are not yet live.
- **Every auto-approval is audited.** A covered escalation appends a
  `grant_applied` ticket event (`toolName`, `callId`, `grant`, `mode`,
  `target`) before answering `allowed-once`; the board's event feed shows
  each one. If the audit event cannot be written, the ask goes to the human
  instead of being answered silently.

The planner is coached to gather evidence for its grants: for every declared
path it runs the read-only `test -w <path>` and records `{path, check,
observed}` in `sandbox.checks`, so the human approves against what was
actually observed rather than an assumption (the KAN-17 `~/dsh-lab` and
KAN-29 `/tmp` classes of surprise). Platform temp areas are already writable
under `workspace-write` and need no grant.

## Config

<!-- verify-allow: config-documented -->

Everything below lives on the `kanban` row.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dbPath` | SQLite file; default `$DSH_HOME/kanban/kanban.db`. |
| `defaultWorkspaceCwd` | cwd for a ticket with no workspace. |
| `providers[]` | `{name, tier: local\|paid, priceIn, priceOut, priceCacheRead, priceCacheWrite}`. |
| `roles{}` | `planner`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `approver`; each has `provider`, `model`, `reasoningEffort`. A null route falls back to the host default model. `allowTools` is still accepted but deprecated and ignored (warned at boot): Kanban registers no tool guard. |
| `confidenceThreshold` | default `0.70`. |
| `allowTicketThresholdOverride` | whether a ticket may carry its own threshold. |
| `maxAttempts` | implement/review rounds before `needs_attention`. |
| `escalationLadder[]` | attempt-to-route overrides. |
| `tickIntervalMs` | worker tick (default 5000). |
| `stallTimeoutMs` | idle turn timeout (default 10 min); suspended while a native question waits. |
| `wipCap` | maximum workflow turns the engine drives concurrently (a pure throttle — queued Working tickets wait, nothing is rejected). |
| `defaultPlanTiming` | `now` or `at_pickup`. |
| `defaultPlanQuestions` | `interactive` or `autonomous`. |
| `defaultBudgetUsd`, `retentionDays`, `promptsDir` | budget, artifact retention, prompt directory. |

Prompts are markdown files under `prompts/`: `plan-human.md`, `plan-self.md`,
`implement.md`, `rework.md`, `review.md`, `approval.md`. Their hashes are recorded
on runs and spans.

A prompt says the job and nothing the session can already see. Plan and build
prompts open a fresh session, so they carry the full ticket, plan and conditions.
Review, rework and approval run inside the build session that wrote the code, so
they do not repaste the plan, the implementation JSON or the diff: the review
prompt names the condition ids it must be answered with and the exact shape of
`kanban_submit_review`, and the approval prompt is one line asking the agent to
offer the human their next steps.

Config reload is atomic through `configEditor`; an invalid reload keeps the
previous config.

## Roles

A role is a model route and a phase — not a tool list. Every role session gets
its preset's tools (standard for plan and verify, the ticket's choice for
build), and all six Kanban action tools are registered in
every workflow session, whichever purpose it belongs to. Each submitting tool
enforces its own phase and refuses a call that does not belong to it, so a
session that changes phase (implement → review) or is reattached after a restart
never finds the tool it needs missing. `kanban_plan` is read-only and gated by
nothing.

| Role | Purpose | Sandbox mode | Action tools that accept a call |
|---|---|---|---|
| `planner` | plan | read-only | `kanban_submit_plan` |
| `implementer` | build | workspace-write | `kanban_submit_implementation` |
| `reviewer` | build | workspace-write | `kanban_submit_review` |
| `approver` | build | workspace-write | `kanban_approve`, `kanban_discard`, `kanban_submit_plan` |
| any | plan or build | — | `kanban_plan` (read-only, every phase) |

A misdirected call is an ordinary tool error the model can read and correct, and
the engine re-validates the ticket's own phase before it records anything, so a
call made in the right session but the wrong ticket state still fails cleanly. A
`done_when` array whose ids are not the plan's is rejected the same way, at the
tool boundary, with the expected ids named in the error.

## Lifecycle

```text
phase:  plan → implement → review → approval → closed
column: backlog | working | done | discarded        (intended state, all grey)
status: idle | active | attention                  (computed per card, never stored)
```

- The engine drives every **Working** ticket as far as its phase allows, plus
  **Backlog** tickets whose Planning is `now` — those plan in place and stop at
  Build until a human drags them to Working.
- Plan runs immediately for `now`, or when the ticket enters Working for
  `at_pickup`.
- Review pass is checked against the plan/acceptance by code and then moves to
  `approval`, where the ticket parks with an attention card wherever it stands.
- Approval is the build session's third phase. The engine flips that session to
  the approver phase and route and sends it one slim hand-over prompt; the agent
  summarizes and asks. You can answer it there, or use **Approve and close** /
  **Discard** on the card. `kanban_submit_plan` there starts another
  implement/review round in the same column.
- Dragging a ticket between Backlog and Working is an unconditional human
  statement of intent: into Working starts (or resumes) the engine and lifts any
  park; back into Backlog stops it. There is no Blocked column and no automatic
  promotion.
- Historical tickets/sessions are discarded by the schema V3 reset. Schema V4
  renames the column set in place: `now` → `working`, and `needs_attention` /
  `blocked` → `backlog` (a parked ticket keeps its reason and still glows red).

## Model routing

The top-right **Model routing** dialog edits each role's base route through
`configEditor.edit`. The picker is one provider-grouped list sourced from the
host model catalog.

Next to each model picker is a **reasoning effort** picker. Its options are
**Default** plus the levels the selected model actually offers, read from the
same host catalog the global model settings use (`reasoning.efforts` on the
model's resolved info — for a hand-declared provider route that is its declared
`reasoningEfforts`). Labels come from the catalog too, so the dialog can never
offer a level the provider has not declared.

- **Default** stores `reasoningEffort: null`, which means "ask the model": the
  harness applies the model's own default, and an escalation rung or the
  deployment default model may still supply one. Choosing Default clears a
  level saved earlier instead of leaving it behind.
- A model with no reasoning metadata shows **no effort control at all** — there
  is nothing to pick. Switching a role to such a model, or to one that does not
  offer the level you had picked, resets that draft back to Default — and a row
  that *starts* edit carrying a level its model no longer offers (a hand-edited
  row, or a backend swap that dropped the model's reasoning metadata) drops it
  the same way, so one stale level cannot block the save of the other roles.
- Saving validates every non-null level against the live catalog and answers
  `bad_request` naming the role, the model and the levels it offers. A level
  that cannot be checked because the provider is unreachable is rejected rather
  than guessed at.
- At boot and on config reload a level the catalog no longer offers is a
  **warning**, not a failure: the request path already rejects it with
  `UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT`, and a provider-config swap must not take the
  profile down.

The written row looks like any other role route:

```yaml
- id: kanban
  config:
    roles:
      implementer: { provider: local-ai-machine, model: big-moe, reasoningEffort: xhigh }
```

## Telemetry

Spans record role, provider/model, attempt, timing, status and prompt hash;
usage records tokens and cost. Timeline blocks are plugin/phase steps, with
expandable prompt/result/plan/review artifacts and lifecycle
events. JSONL/CSV exports and analytics remain available.

## Board and chat surface

A card is **blue and softly glowing** while its ticket has a turn in flight, and
**static red** when it needs attention — border, tint, left accent bar and a red
status dot, no pulsing. Attention is a state to read, not a light to chase. A
red card whose session is paused mid-turn on a person says so in its badge —
**Awaiting approval** for an unanswered approval prompt, **Waiting on you** for
an unanswered question — in any phase, not only in approval.

Clicking a card opens the ticket detail. Nothing in the board ever opens a
session by itself: watching the poll, or clicking through a ticket that is
planning, building or reviewing, never navigates you out of the board. The
explicit buttons still do — **Open build session** on the approval panel,
**Open session** in the detail hero while a mid-turn wait is pending (it lands
you on the prompt itself), **Open** in the sessions table, **Recover tools** on
an orphaned session.

A Backlog ticket usually plans when you drag it into Working. **Start planning**
is the exception you can make without moving it: a small button on the card, and
the same one beside the pencil in the detail hero, sets that ticket's planning to
*now* and lets the engine run the plan session right there in Backlog. When the
plan lands the ticket is still in Backlog, now at **Build** — planning and
building stay two separate decisions, and dragging it over is still what starts
the work. The button shows only where it would do something: a Backlog ticket
still at the plan phase, not already planning now, not mid-turn, and not waiting
on your answer. On a parked plan ticket it doubles as the retry — pressing it
again lifts the park and launches a fresh plan. Behind it is a `startPlanning`
action on the `action` endpoint; it writes `planTiming` and nothing else, and
refuses any other ticket with `bad_request`.

A ticket is edited through the one pencil in the detail hero, which opens a
single editor for the whole card: title, body, acceptance (one statement per
line — change a line to edit it, delete a line to remove it), planning,
questions, priority, allow-paid, budget and workspace, saved in one `update`
call. That pencil is locked the moment the ticket has started in any way: moved
off the plan phase or out of Backlog/Working, an attempt or any spend recorded,
parked for attention, or any session, run, span or condition attached to it. A
locked ticket answers `ticket_started` from `update`, `addAcceptance` and
`setAcceptance`; the engine's own writes (reorder, worktree creation, a retry
patch) go past the lock, because they go straight to the store. Editing a
pristine ticket never locks it — you can fix a card as often as you like before
something starts work on it. An acceptance change is recorded as an
`acceptance_set` event carrying both the prior and the new list, so the words a
human removed stay readable in the audit trail.

In a kanban session's chat, a turn that ended on a `kanban_*` call gets one line
at the turn tail, below the "Completed in …" disclosure, naming the transition
that turn caused: plan submitted, implementation submitted, review not finished
(with the reviewer's feedback), review passed, approved or discarded. Neither
source is enough on its own. The call alone cannot tell an accepted submission
from one a phase gate refused, so the ticket's real phase is checked through the
`sessionInfo` endpoint. The phase alone cannot tell a failed review from a later
passed one in the same session, and would print **Review passed** on the turn
that failed — so the verdict and feedback the call itself carried decide *which*
transition to look for, a pass is only claimed when the ticket's latest review is
the one that call submitted, and a pass is only called unfinished when the host
reports that the review was actually sent back (`reviewRejected`, derived from
artifact ordering) rather than that the ticket happens to sit in `implement`
again. When the two do not agree, nothing is rendered. Long values are truncated
to one line and the full text is in the hover tooltip.

## Ticket images

A ticket body can carry images. In both the New-ticket dialog and the ticket
editor, paste a screenshot into the body box, drop image files onto it, or use
**Add image**: each accepted file gets a thumbnail tile under the box and a
markdown reference inserted at the cursor. The X on a tile removes the tile and
its reference together. Limits: png, jpeg, webp or gif, 20 MB each, at most 10
images per ticket; a rejected paste or drop says why and leaves the text alone.

What is stored is a reference, not the bytes:

```markdown
![screenshot.png](kanban-image:sha256:4f3a…)
```

The bytes live in DSH core's content-addressed attachment store
(`$DSH_HOME/attachments/v1/objects/xx/<sha256>`), so they are validated,
deduplicated, and survive restarts. The body stays the single source of truth —
no extra table, no migration, and **no new config keys**. While you are typing,
the reference carries a temporary `pending-<token>` id; on save the Host stores
each image and rewrites every pending token to its real id before the body is
written. If any image fails to store, or a pending token has no upload behind
it, nothing is written: no ticket is created and no patch is applied.

The ticket detail's **Body** panel renders the body as light markdown —
headings, lists, code, links — and resolves each reference to a real `<img>`
through the `readImage` endpoint. A reference whose bytes no longer resolve
renders as an *image unavailable* chip rather than vanishing.

Role sessions see the images too: a plan session's ticket block ends with an
**Attached images** section listing each image's host file path, and the
session's `read_image` tool works on those paths. Editing a started ticket is
locked by the same rule as any other edit (`ticket_started`).

## Auto-recovery of a halted turn

A role turn can halt for reasons that have nothing to do with the work: the
output-token limit mid-answer, a backend that dropped, a restart that orphaned
the turn. Before 0.4.0 that parked the ticket, and the session sat asleep until
somebody opened it — at which point [dsh-continue-kicker]'s reopen door kicked it
awake *outside* the workflow, so the board said "needs attention" while the
session was actually still working.

Now the engine recovers it inside the workflow. When a plan, implement, review or
approval turn fails, kanban asks the `continueKicker` service that plugin
provides for one explicit kick (`kick(sessionId, { bypassCooldown: true })`),
waits for the
turn it starts, and takes the structured submission from that turn exactly as it
would from one it prompted itself. The ticket keeps its attention card off
(blue, active) throughout; nothing parks until recovery stops.

**The policy is not duplicated here.** What counts as a kickable halt, which
message is sent, and how many kicks in a row still count as recovery rather than
a loop (`maxConsecutiveKicks`) all live in continue-kicker; kanban pulls the
trigger and stops the moment it is declined. A kick that the runaway guard
refuses, a halt it will not kick (an explicit abort), or a turn that stalls after
the kick all park the ticket with the reason it would have had before —
`turn failed in implement: max-tokens` and friends. Each recovered turn is
recorded as a `<phase>-continuation` span with its own usage, so a recovery round
is visible and costed, and it does not consume an attempt.

**The integration is optional and detected, never required.** The service is
resolved lazily and duck-typed (`typeof ctx.get('continueKicker')?.kick ===
'function'`), the same way the worktree integration treats
`betterGitWorktree`. Without the plugin installed kanban logs one line at boot —
`dsh-continue-kicker not mounted; halted turns park to needs-attention without
auto-recovery` — and behaves exactly as in 0.3.x. `GET /api/kanban/capabilities`
reports `continueKicker: true|false` alongside `worktree`. A recovery kick shows
up on the ticket timeline as an `auto_recovered` event carrying the phase, the
halt flavor and the kick number.

## Worktrees

A ticket can ask to be worked in its own git working copy, and the ask is
**intent, not an action**: the new-ticket **Worktree** switch writes
`tickets.worktree` and creates nothing. The copy is settled when a plan session
actually starts, which is the moment the question "where should this work?" first
has an answer.

At plan start the driver asks `dsh-better-git-worktree` for the directory, in
three shapes:

- **The ticket already points at a checkout** (every ticket made before 0.14.0,
  and any workspace a human picked). If that path is a managed working copy it is
  fetched and fast-forwarded onto the latest default branch — but only when the
  copy is *pristine*: a clean tree including untracked paths, and no commit the
  commit it was cut from does not already have. A copy with work in it is left
  exactly as it is, and the plan prompt gains a line saying so, naming the path,
  the branch, why it was not moved and what it is based on. Nothing is ever
  deleted, reset or rebased.
- **The ticket only recorded the intent.** The copy is created now, from the
  just-fetched `origin/<default branch>` (not from wherever the source checkout
  happens to sit), registered as a workspace, and the ticket is re-pointed at it.
  A later phase, or a re-plan, takes the first branch above.
- **Neither.** The ordinary default workspace, exactly as before.

A `git fetch` that fails **fails the plan dispatch**: the ticket parks in
needs-attention carrying git's own words, because planning against a base nobody
could bring up to date is the one thing the switch was asked to prevent. With
`dsh-better-git-worktree` not mounted at all, the switch is hidden, the intent is
ignored with one log line, and planning behaves as it always did.

The `worktree` endpoint on the `action` route stays as the manual escape hatch
(create a copy for a ticket right now); the create form no longer calls it.

## Restart safety

Running spans are abandoned on restart; affected tickets park in place with a
needs-attention reason (their column is untouched), and their workflow sessions
are closed so continue-kicker does not resume a dead Kanban session.

[dsh-continue-kicker]: https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tree/main/packages/continue-kicker#provided-service-continuekicker

# dsh-plugins

Public [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) plugins by [Chris Johnson](https://github.com/chrisjohnson). One repository, independently installable plugins — each with its own README, its own tests, its own changelog and its own version.

## Install

**Nothing here is published to npm.** Every release is a git tag on this repository, named `<package>-v<version>` (for example `dsh-model-switch-v0.2.1`), and you install a plugin by pinning that tag plus the package's subdirectory:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#<package>-v<version>&path:/packages/<dir>"
```

`dsh plugin add` hands that spec to pnpm and also lists the package under the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, which is what activates its configuration layer. If you manage a profile's `package.json` yourself, the same spec works with pnpm directly — but then add the package name to `dsh.profile.bundles` by hand, because a plain `pnpm add` installs the plugin without enabling it:

```sh
pnpm add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#<package>-v<version>&path:/packages/<dir>"
```

Pick the tag from [the repository's tags](https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tags); `<dir>` is the folder under `packages/` in the index below.

> **Warning — do not install these by bare name.** `pnpm add dsh-model-switch` (or `dsh plugin add dsh-model-switch`) resolves against the npm registry, and the npm package called `dsh-model-switch` belongs to an unrelated author: it is **not** this plugin. The same can happen to any unscoped `dsh-*` name. Always use the git-tag spec above.

## Index

| Plugin | What it is for | Latest | Directory |
| --- | ---

# dsh-loop-watchdog

**A stuck-session signal for agents you leave running — an audit ledger first, an intervention only if you ask for one.**

A host plugin for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) that checks a session before each agent step and writes one record per check saying whether it looks stuck, with the evidence. It ships a panel (for `dsh-better-sidebar`) that draws that ledger for the current session.

Precision over recall. A false positive tells a working agent to abandon its strategy; a false negative costs a few minutes. So the watchdog is built around evidence that cannot hallucinate, and what it does about a verdict is off until you turn it on.

| Layer | What it does | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Repetition check** (deterministic) | Hashes `(tool, normalised arguments)` over the last `fpWindowEvents` events. The same call repeated with *no new information* is stuck: 3 or more repeats with at most one distinct result, or 5 or more with at most two. | No model call. |
| **Model adjudication** (optional) | For windows the first layer did not settle, asks a model you configure whether the last few steps produced **new information** (a new file read, a new error, a result that differs) or re-ran work that already failed. It answers `LOOP:N` or `PROGRESS:N`. | One small completion, at most once per `cooldownMs`, skipped while the previous one was slow. |
| **Intervention** (off by default) | In the *stuck* band, sustained over two consecutive checks, in act mode, once per stuck episode: steers one non-destructive note into the session asking the agent to state what it has established and take the cheapest check that could falsify its approach. | One message. |

Similar-looking commands with new results are progress; the same command returning the same nothing is a loop. That distinction is the whole design.

## Install

Installed from a git tag of this repository — it is not published to npm. Replace `<version>` with a released version (tags are named `dsh-loop-watchdog-v<version>`; see [the tag list](https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins/tags)):

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-loop-watchdog-v<version>&path:/packages/loop-watchdog"
```

That installs the package into the profile and enables its bundle. If you manage the profile's `package.json` yourself, the pnpm equivalent is below — then also add `dsh-loop-watchdog` to the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles`, because `pnpm add` alone installs the plugin without enabling it:

```sh
pnpm add "git+https://github.com/chrisjohnson/dsh-plugins.git#dsh-loop-watchdog-v<version>&path:/packages/loop-watchdog"
```

> **Warning:** never `pnpm add dsh-loop-watchdog` (or `dsh plugin add dsh-loop-watchdog`) by bare name. That resolves from the npm registry, where an unscoped `dsh-*` name can belong to an unrelated author and is **not** this plugin.

Restart dsh. With no configuration the repetition check runs, every check is ledgered, and nothing intervenes. Model adjudication stays off until you give it an endpoint and a model (below), and the boot log says so.

## Configuration

Set these on the row in your own profile patch (`config:` block). **A patch layer replaces a row's whole `config` object**, so a row that sets one key must restate every key it wants to differ from the default.

| Key | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `interventionEnabled` | `false` | Whether to steer a sustained-stuck session. Log-only by default. The [mode file](#the-mode-file) overrides this at runtime. |
| `llmBaseUrl` | *unset* | Base URL of an OpenAI-compatible API; `/chat/completions` is appended. **Unset (or `llmModel` unset) turns model adjudication off**: the repetition check still runs, and ambiguous windows are ledgered as skipped (`no-llm`). |
| `llmModel` | *unset* | Model id sent to that endpoint. |
| `llmApiKeyEnv` | *unset* | The **name** of the environment variable that holds the API key — never the key. Read at call time. Unset, or an empty variable, sends no `Authorization` header (the boot log warns for the empty case). |
| `llmExtraBody` | `{}` | Extra fields merged under the request body, for a backend-specific switch — for example `chat_template_kwargs: {enable_thinking: false}` to stop a thinking model reasoning before a one-line answer. The fixed fields (`model`, `max_tokens`, `temperature: 0`, `messages`) win. |
| `llmMaxTokens` | `128` | Completion budget for the one-line verdict. |
| `ledgerFile` | `$DSH_HOME/storages/loop-watchdog/evaluations.jsonl` | The [evaluation ledger](#the-ledger). Always written. A relative value resolves against `$DSH_HOME`. |
| `modeFile` | `$DSH_HOME/storages/loop-watchdog/mode.json` | The runtime act/log override. This plugin only reads it. A relative value resolves against `$DSH_HOME`. |
| `cooldownMs` | `30000` | Minimum gap between two evaluations of one session. |
| `maxTranscriptLines` | `6` | Substantive events shown to the model (and recorded in the ledger window). |
| `fpWindowEvents` | `60` | Raw events the repetition check scans (~15 tool calls). |
| `watchdogTimeoutMs` | `25000` | Abort a model call after this long. The check fails open. |
| `busyYieldMs` | `15000` | After a model call slower than this, the next model check is skipped so the watchdog does not compete with the session it supervises. |
| `bandStuck` / `bandWatch` | `90` / `70` | Confidence thresholds for the `stuck` (actionable) and `watch` bands, for a `LOOP` verdict. Anything lower, or any `PROGRESS` verdict, is `noise`. |
| `includeSubagents` | `false` | Subagent sessions are skipped unless this is `true`. |
| `logFile` | `true` | Write the verbose stage trail to `logFilePath`. **The trail includes the transcript window sent to the model, so tool output and file contents land in that file by default**; set `false` if the log directory is not as private as the session. |
| `logFilePath` | `$DSH_HOME/storages/loop-watchdog/watchdog.log` | Where that trail goes. Relative values resolve against `$DSH_HOME`. |
| `logConsole` | `false` | Also print the trail to stdout (the journal under systemd). Off because it fires on every step of every session. |
| `logDsh` | `false` | Send the trail to dsh's own logger. |
| `logDshErrors` | `true` | Keep genuine errors on dsh's logger even when `logDsh` is off. |

`$DSH_HOME` is the environment variable when set (blank counts as unset), else `~/.dsh`, resolved the way the harness resolves it (a leading `~` expands). Every path key accepts an absolute path (used verbatim), a `~` path, or a path **relative to `$DSH_HOME`** — never relative to the working directory. `watchdogTimeoutMs` and `llmMaxTokens` must be above zero. A `llmBaseUrl` with a query string warns, and the logged endpoint never carries credentials or a query. Resolution lives in [`src/config.mjs`](./src/config.mjs) and is [tested](./test/config.test.mjs); a misspelled key, a YAML `"30000"`, a base URL that is not http(s), or a model with no endpoint each print one warning at boot.

Example, on a deployment with a local OpenAI-compatible gateway:

```yaml
- id: loop-watchdog
  name: dsh-loop-watchdog
  config:
    llmBaseUrl: http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1
    llmModel: small-model
    llmApiKeyEnv: GATEWAY_API_KEY
    llmExtraBody:
      chat_template_kwargs:
        enable_thinking: false
    interventionEnabled: false
```

## The ledger

Every evaluation appends one JSON line to `ledgerFile` (schema `v: 2`), carrying both layers:

- `code` — the repetition check's full result, including "ran, scanned N calls, found nothing", which decides nothing and would otherwise leave no trace;
- `model` — the model's verdict, present only when the first layer was inconclusive and the model was consulted;
- `verdict`, `confidence`, `band`, `streak`, `mode`, `outcome` (`logged`, `intervened`, `intervene-error`, `skipped`), the matched `fingerprints`, latency, and the exact transcript `window` that was judged.

Steps deliberately not evaluated are recorded too, but **only the first of a stretch** (a stretch of a different kind in between, such as a cooldown, starts a new one), so the ledger does not gain a row every few seconds: `no-signal` (fewer than two substantive events), `cooldown`, `busy` (the previous model check was slow), and `no-llm` (nothing left to ask). A real evaluation ends the stretch.

### Existing history: pointing at the old locations

The defaults above are this package's own directory. A deployment that already ran the original in-tree watchdog has history and a mode toggle elsewhere, and **without the mapping the watchdog starts a new empty ledger and ignores the old toggle**. Either set the keys (relative to `$DSH_HOME`):

```yaml
    ledgerFile: storages/semantic-loop-kicker/evaluations.jsonl
    modeFile: profiles/web/watchdog-mode.json
```

or move the old data once — `mv $DSH_HOME/storages/semantic-loop-kicker $DSH_HOME/storages/loop-watchdog` (the file inside keeps its name, `evaluations.jsonl`) — and leave the keys unset. Remove the old in-tree rows in the same change: two watchers appending to one ledger would double every record.

The file is the interface. Anything may read it; the evals panel is one reader. Older `v: 1` (decisions-only) lines stay readable: the reader normalises them into the current shape. The watchdog never rotates or truncates it.

## The mode file

`interventionEnabled` is the default. Whatever UI or script you like can override it at runtime by writing `modeFile`:

```json
{ "interventionEnabled": true }
```

The file is read on **every check**, so a toggle takes effect within one cooldown window, no restart. Absent, unreadable, or without a boolean `interventionEnabled` means "no override". This plugin never writes the file and ships no toggle UI of its own.

## The evals panel

The same package serves a read-only view of the ledger to a `dsh-better-sidebar` tab, "Loop evals": a timing graph with a code lane, a model lane and a dim skip lane, a synced ledger list, and a detail view of one evaluation (fingerprint groups, the model's raw reply, latency, the transcript window). It defaults to the current session, with a toggle for all.

`dsh-better-sidebar` is an **optional** integration. The panel module declares that service as a requirement, so without better-sidebar installed it stays inactive and registers nothing; the watchdog and its ledger are unaffected. It uses better-sidebar 0.25.0's `ctx.betterSidebar.registerTab(descriptor)`, whose registration is disposed with this plugin's fiber. The panel reads the ledger through a plugin-owned route, `/loopWatchdog/<list|sessions|detail>`, behind the connection service's trust check.

## Session format V4

Dsh 0.2.0 sessions are format V4, and the watchdog reads V4 events: a `user/message` event's `data` **is** the message; a `tool/result` event's `data.message` is a first-class `{role: 'tool', toolCallId, content}` message, whose text is its content blocks. The steering note is written with source kind `plugin:loop-watchdog` — V4 refuses the bare kind `plugin` on read, so a session carrying such a message could not be reopened after a restart.

## Failure modes

- **Fails open, always.** A model timeout, HTTP error or unparseable reply yields no verdict (band `noise`) and the turn proceeds. A thrown error is logged and never reaches the agent loop; the `agent/pre-step` listener awaits the waterfall first and runs the check without blocking it.
- **No model configured:** the repetition check still decides on its own; ambiguous windows are ledgered as `no-llm`.
- **Ledger or log not writable:** writes are best effort and silently skipped; the agent is never affected.
- **A model that reasons before answering** may spend `llmMaxTokens` on thinking and return nothing; pass the backend's switch in `llmExtraBody`.

## Compatibility

Requires dsh 0.2.0-rc.2 or later. Declared in `package.json` under `engines.dsh` and on the `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` peer as `>=0.2.0-rc.2 <0.3.0-0 || >=0.3.0-0`. dsh checks these ranges itself, counting prereleases; pnpm's own peer check is narrower and may report a mismatch on other prereleases that dsh does not.

## Troubleshooting

**Nothing is ever ledgered.** The ledger needs at least two substantive events and a clear cooldown. Check `logFilePath` for `[B]` lines: `skip … only N substantive events` or `COOLDOWN_SKIP` say why.

**Every ambiguous window is a `no-llm` skip.** Model adjudication is off. The boot log names the keys: `llmBaseUrl` and `llmModel`.

**The panel tab is missing.** `dsh-better-sidebar` is not installed or not yet loaded. Check the browser console for a `loop-watchdog` line, and that better-sidebar's own tab bar works.

**The panel says "ledger-missing".** The watchdog has not written yet, or the panel and the host disagree on `ledgerFile` — they read the same row's config, so check that the path exists and is writable by the dsh user.

## Development

Plain ESM, no build step:

```sh
node --test packages/loop-watchdog/test/*.test.mjs    # decisions, reading V4 events, ledger, config, client contract
node scripts/verify.mjs --package dsh-loop-watchdog   # release contract
node scripts/compose-smoke.mjs loop-watchdog          # real dsh composition
node scripts/check-plugin-hooks.mjs                   # React hook-order gate for the client half
```
